reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because its primary content is conditional Dogecoin technical analysis that identifies support, resistance, and upside targets while stating that the bullish view should be reassessed if support breaks. Although it includes paid-signal promotion and an invitation to join for free signals, the available video evidence describes no deceptive terms, guaranteed returns, payment requirements, losses, or improper connection to the analysis, and notes an educational disclaimer.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the proposed trade and the invitation together. The speaker says repeated moves from support have been at least 4% to 6% and connects that pattern to profitable strategies. He then invites viewers to join for signals. That makes the projected upside more than detached commentary: it gives viewers a reason to enter a signals channel to act on DOGE. The evidence does not prove anyone bought DOGE or earned a return, but the return language and participation invitation appear in the same pitch.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the targets are conditional, but a condition does not separate the analysis from the solicitation. Its cited paid group is part of the concern: viewers hear that recurring moves can build profitable strategies while being offered signals to trade on. No payment requirement or guaranteed return has to be inferred to recognize that connection. The break-below-support warning qualifies the pitch; it does not remove the invitation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited percentages are a claim about past price moves, not a promise that joining signals or buying DOGE will produce them. The speaker expressly says the bullish view fails if support breaks, and the opening disclaimer warns that trading can lose the entire investment. A promotional link alongside conditional market analysis does not establish a deceptive token-purchase offer.

The description offers a paid signals group, while the chart repeatedly displays a free-signals invitation. Even without an explicit guarantee, this presentation can make a speculative DOGE trade look unusually dependable and direct viewers toward a trading-signals channel.

Those qualifications matter when judging whether the signals invitation is a scam rather than promotion attached to market commentary.

The proposed upside targets give that invitation a practical purpose: viewers are being shown a trade idea and then pointed toward an ongoing source of signals. Calling the video educational does not settle what role this repeated promotion plays.
